analysis.one_liner: Declares a right to a job at living wages and directs federal policy toward full employment and shorter hours.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to four House committees and four subcommittees in 1995 and never received a hearing, a vote, or any action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill declares an updated 'economic bill of rights': every adult who wants to work should have access to a job at decent pay, and anyone who cannot work or find a job should have an adequate standard of living. It would bar federal agencies, including the Federal Reserve, from promoting recession or unemployment as a way to hold down wages or inflation, set a goal of cutting unemployment to 3 percent for adults within three years, and require a presidential program using public works, lower interest rates, triple overtime pay beyond 40 hours, and a 35-hour maximum workweek in manufacturing and mining to get there. It would also require the annual budget to spell out who gains and loses from federal spending, and put the Joint Economic Committee in charge of checking whether the White House and federal agencies are following through.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers and job seekers gain the most: the bill commits the government to pushing unemployment toward 3 percent for adults, pays triple time for hours beyond 40 a week, cuts the manufacturing and mining workweek to 35 hours without a pay cut, and expands part-time jobs with benefits. Low-wage workers, people facing hiring discrimination, and workers trying to unionize are singled out for new rights and federal support.

how_it_helps.text: Sets a legal goal of reducing unemployment to 3 percent for adults within three years, using public works, infrastructure repair, and reduced interest rates to put jobless people to work
Prohibits federal agencies and the Federal Reserve from directly or indirectly promoting recession, stagnation, or unemployment as a means of reducing wages or inflation

Requires triple-time pay for hours over 40 per week and cuts the manufacturing and mining workweek to 35 hours with no loss in weekly wages, while banning compulsory overtime and extending paid vacations
Reaffirms the right to organize and bargain collectively, and directs the federal government to actively support that right in other countries
Requires every presidential budget to disclose who gains and who loses from federal spending, including tax breaks and per-state and per-district flows of federal money

analysis.who_pays: Employers would bear higher labor costs from triple overtime pay, the 35-hour manufacturing workweek, and pressure toward full-employment wage growth. The Federal Reserve would give up discretion to fight inflation by allowing unemployment to rise. Taxpayers fund whatever the authorized job-creation and social programs cost, which the bill leaves open-ended ('such sums as may be necessary').

drawbacks.text: The appropriations are open-ended — 'such sums as may be necessary' — so the cost of the guaranteed-jobs program and its benefits is not specified anywhere in the bill

The bill orders the Federal Reserve to stop using unemployment to restrain inflation and sets a 3 percent unemployment goal within three years, which mainstream economics warns could allow inflation to accelerate and is a pace no country has reliably sustained

Triple-time overtime premiums and a mandatory 35-hour manufacturing week without pay cuts raise employer costs sharply, and the bill's answer to business objections is largely 'tripartite' labor-government-business bargaining rather than any transition relief

Most of the bill is declarations of rights and reporting duties; the concrete enforcement mechanism is limited to Joint Economic Committee reports and annual goals, so many of the rights it proclaims would depend on future Congresses funding and enforcing them

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The goals are ambitious: genuine full employment, shorter hours at no pay loss, and a budget that tells the public who benefits from federal money. The costs are real but unquantified — the bill never estimates what its job programs cost, and its directive to the Federal Reserve collides with the standard tool of inflation control. Its biggest weakness is design: it proclaims rights without building most of the machinery to deliver them, leaving the heavy lifting to appropriations and future action that this bill cannot compel.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to four House committees the day it was introduced, then split among four subcommittees over the next two months, and none of them ever held a hearing or voted on it — the bill died quietly when the Congress ended in January 1997.

narrative.text: Ron Dellums introduced the Living Wage, Jobs For All Act on February 24, 1995, with 17 colleagues joining at introduction
The bill drew 29 cosponsors — 28 Democrats and one Independent — but no Republicans
The Speaker referred it to four committees: Economic and Educational Opportunities, Government Reform and Oversight, Budget, and Rules
Between February 28 and April 27, 1995, it was split across four subcommittees — Government Management, Workforce Protections, Employer-Employee Relations, and the Legislative and Budget Process
No further action of any kind appears in the record through the end of the 104th Congress on January 3, 1997

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who would have paid the triple-overtime premium and the shorter manufacturing workweek are better off, as is the Federal Reserve, which keeps its independence to manage inflation through interest rates. The 104th Congress's committee leaders are better off in the sense that they never had to take a position on a bill that would have committed the government to a guaranteed right to a job.

for.name: Rep. Ron Dellums
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to establish a living wage and jobs-for-all policy and to reduce poverty and the concentration of income and wealth

for.name: 29 House cosponsors
for.role: Cosponsors, including Reps. Bonior, Conyers, Pelosi, Rangel, and Sanders (I)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; every cosponsor was a Democrat except one Independent

against.name: Committee on Economic and Educational Opportunities
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day it was introduced and never reported it out or held a recorded hearing

against.name: Committees on Government Reform and Oversight, Budget, and Rules
against.what_they_did: Also received the bill on introduction; none took further action on it

sides.party_line_note: All 29 cosponsors were Democrats except one Independent; no Republican cosponsored, and no vote was ever taken, so the bill never faced a recorded partisan test.

industries.industry: Employers, especially manufacturers and mining companies
industries.note: The bill would require triple-time pay past 40 hours a week, cap manufacturing and mining weeks at 35 hours with no wage cut, and push wages up through a full-employment mandate. Its higher labor costs are exactly the wages and hours gains ordinary workers would receive.

The bill would order the Fed to stop promoting recession or unemployment to hold down inflation and to plan its policy around a 3 percent unemployment goal. That constrains the Fed's independence, which defenders say protects price stability that benefits everyone, while supporters see it as ending a policy that trades workers' jobs for lower inflation.

Every presidential budget would have to show who gains and loses from federal spending, break out operating versus investment spending, and itemize tax breaks and per-district federal flows. The tradeoff is that the bill's own job programs carry open-ended, unspecified costs.
